finding: §2.1's back-compat sentence claims that on an older tp `enabled: false` "is rejected as an unpermitted key and ignored, so the role stays active and the user is told why". The second half does not hold on the path that matters. The unpermitted-key text is a parser warning appended to `Frontmatter.Warnings` (internal/engine/frontmatter.go:163), and `fm.Warnings` has exactly one consumer in the repo: internal/cli/lint.go:92, i.e. `tp lint`. Neither `tp review` nor `tp audit` reads it — their emission path prints only the `ResolveActiveCorpus` / `ResolveOverrideFocus` warnings via `output.Info` (internal/cli/review.go:657-665). So an older tp running `tp review`/`tp audit` on a v0.32.0 spec silently emits the full panel including the role the spec meant to deactivate, and says nothing unless the user separately runs `tp lint`. This is the spec's only stated graceful-degradation story for older binaries, and it promises a notification tp does not deliver on the command where the deactivation is ignored. Note the same channel split makes §2.2's new non-boolean-`enabled` warning invisible during emission, which is correct as written (§2.2 says "lint warning") — only §2.1's trailing clause overclaims.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §2.1 no longer claims the older tp tells the user why: its message names the permitted set as `(only focus)`, which says the key was refused but not that a newer tp would honor it. The spec now says exactly that.

suggestion: Name the channel and its limit in §2.1: "On an older tp, `enabled: false` is an unpermitted key and is ignored, so the role stays active; `tp lint` reports it, but `tp review`/`tp audit` do not surface frontmatter shape warnings, so on those commands the deactivation is silently absent." If surfacing it on the emission path is wanted, that is a separate change to how `fm.Warnings` is plumbed and belongs in §5 as an explicit Non-Goal rather than as an implied guarantee.

finding: The empty-phase message's id list is unpinned in the mixed case, which is reachable and is the case an implementer is most likely to get wrong. §2.5 renders '... deactivated by this spec: architect, tester' with '(the ids sorted and comma-separated)' and item 7 says 'the deactivated ids' — but §1 states that `domains` also 'deactivates a role per spec', so when a corpus of {a, b} has b removed by `domains` and a dropped by `enabled: false`, the phase is empty and two engineers render two different messages: '…: a' (the §2.3 drop set) or '…: a, b' (every id absent from the active set). Item 7's fixture is the pure case (every role deactivated by `enabled: false`), so nothing in §6 discriminates between the two renderings.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §2.5 now pins the mixed case: the list carries only the ids this spec deactivated, not those already absent through `domains` or a missing file.

suggestion: Say in §2.5 that the listed ids are exactly §2.3's drop set and never the `domain-mismatch` ones, and extend item 7 with the mixed fixture — a corpus whose remaining role is domain-filtered and whose only active role is dropped — asserting the message names only the dropped id.

finding: Non-Goal 3 ('`enabled: true` does not resurrect a role removed by `domains`') is a testable behavioral guarantee with no §6 item, and it is the one empty cell of the grid §6 otherwise fills: (true, active) = item 3, (false, active) = item 1, (false, domain-filtered) = item 6's second half, (true, domain-filtered) = nothing. The escape is a natural implementation, not a contrived one: applying the tri-state as 'Enabled==false → drop from the active set; Enabled==true → ensure present from the corpus' satisfies every current §6 item — item 3 only ever sees an already-active role — while breaking Non-Goal 3 silently.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §6 item 13 is new and tests Non-Goal 3 — with the role filtered out by `domains`, `enabled: true` takes the "matches no active role" path and the role stays absent.

suggestion: Extend item 6's second half with the mirror assertion: `enabled: true` on a role removed by `domains` leaves it filtered — absent from the emitted panel and still named in `skipped_roles` with `domain-mismatch` (Non-Goal 3).

finding: §2.2 gained a carve-out this round — `enabled: null` and a valueless `enabled:` decode to nil, are unset, and warn NOT — but §6 adds no item for it, and item 4's rule as written ('A non-boolean `enabled` warns and leaves the role active') reads as covering null, since null is not a boolean. The two engineers split predictably: one writes only the quoted-string fixture item 4 names, the other adds `enabled: null` (and a bare `enabled:`) as a second non-boolean fixture and asserts the `is not a boolean (got %T); ignored` warning — which §2.2 says must not fire. This is also the likelier implementation bug, not a hypothetical: a parser that type-asserts `raw.(bool)` fails the assert on a nil value and emits the warning with `got <nil>`, and no §6 item catches it.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §6 item 14 is new and covers the carve-out: `enabled: null` and a valueless `enabled:` warn not and leave the role active, distinguishing the unset case from item 4's quoted string.

suggestion: Add a §6 item (or a second clause on item 4) pinning the carve-out: `enabled: null` and a valueless `enabled:` leave the role active and emit no warning, while the quoted `enabled: "false"` fixture warns — and reword item 4 as 'a non-boolean, non-null `enabled`' so the two fixtures cannot be read as the same case.

finding: Item 3's repaired reason is false against the tree, and is a strictly worse claim than the one it replaced. internal/engine/lens_shim_test.go builds NO ReviewRoles map literals: every fixture is a YAML string handed to ParseFrontmatterBytes, and the file's only ReviewRoles reference is require.NotEmpty(t, fm.ReviewRoles, "new form parsed") at lens_shim_test.go:60, which compiles unchanged against map[string]RoleOverride. So "the literals are what invalidate it under either branch" is false in BOTH branches. Under the call-site-adaptation branch nothing in the file breaks at all — it compiles and passes, contradicting the section title "Existing tests this change invalidates". Under the returns-new-type branch what breaks is assert.Equal(t, []string{...}, overrides[<id>]) at :22, :34-:36 and :48 — i.e. the TranslateLegacyLens return type, the exact reason round 11 removed as unreliable. Round 10 set the precedent for this class on §6 item 7 ("the inaccurate EnsureReviewState justification is deleted from the item; the assertion stands on its own without explaining the asymmetry through a code claim that was wrong"); this repair swapped in another unverified code claim instead of dropping the justification.

resolved.evidence: CONFIRMED, and my round-11 repair made this entry worse than what it replaced. Verified against the tree: lens_shim_test.go builds NO ReviewRoles map literals — it parses YAML fixtures, reads fm.ReviewRoles once through require.NotEmpty (line 60), and asserts TranslateLegacyLens's return. The entry now says that, and that the file is invalidated only under the signature-change branch.

suggestion: State the branch dependency rather than a fabricated cause: lens_shim_test.go is invalidated only if TranslateLegacyLens returns the new type, in which case its assert.Equal(t, []string{...}, overrides[<id>]) comparisons (lines 22, 34-36, 48) break; under call-site adaptation the file compiles and passes unchanged, so list it conditionally or drop it from a section titled "Existing tests this change invalidates". Before assigning a cause to any of the preamble's four token hits, check whether the hit is a code reference at all.

finding: Item 4 ("internal/cli/domain_lens_test.go — exercises ResolveOverrideFocus through the CLI; moves with its new signature") is verifiably false and the file is not invalidated. That file has zero code references to ResolveOverrideFocus, ReviewRoles or AuditRoles; its only hit is the comment at :189 ("covered by the engine test TestResolveOverrideFocus_UnknownID"). Its two override tests are black-box subprocess runs — runTP(t, dir, "review", "spec.md", "--no-state") at :180 and :195 — asserting on emitted prompts, so they compile and pass unchanged after §2.2's type change and §2.3's third return value, and nothing in them touches enabled. The defect was reported in an earlier round and recorded fixed by a bulk resolution ("Addressed by this round's repairs to §1, §6 item 7, the new item 8, item 9 and item 15") that names no edit to §6.1; the entry is verbatim unchanged. This round §6.1 WAS edited for exactly this class, in the adjacent item 3, and item 4 was left — so a task derived from item 4 still has nothing to do.

resolved.evidence: CONFIRMED, and it also defeats my round-10 WONTFIX on the same entry. I claimed I had verified one code reference; the single occurrence is the comment `// covered by the engine test TestResolveOverrideFocus_UnknownID` at line 189 — I counted a comment. §6.1 item 4 now states the file is NOT invalidated and is listed only so the search's fourth hit is accounted for rather than silently dropped; the preamble says three of four are invalidated.

suggestion: Delete item 4 from the invalidation list, or restate it as a non-invalidating match: domain_lens_test.go is black-box (runTP over emitted prompts) and survives the signature change untouched. If the preamble's "exactly four files" count stays, say the fourth hit is a comment-only match kept for search reproducibility, not a file this change invalidates.

finding: §6.1 item 3 describes `internal/engine/lens_shim_test.go` as one that "builds `ReviewRoles` map literals, whose element type changes", and its parenthetical concludes "so the literals are what invalidate it under either branch." Both halves are false against the file (76 lines, read in full). Its only `ReviewRoles` reference is `require.NotEmpty(t, fm.ReviewRoles, "new form parsed")` at line 60, which compiles and passes under any element type — the file contains no `ReviewRoles` map literal. Every literal it builds (lines 22-23, 34-36, 63, 74) is an assertion over `TranslateLegacyLens`'s returned override map, i.e. precisely the signature §2.2 explicitly leaves to the implementer. The conclusion is therefore inverted: under §2.2's adapt-at-the-call-site branch (TranslateLegacyLens keeps returning `map[string][]string`) this file is not invalidated at all; it is invalidated only under the change-the-return-type branch, and then by the `TranslateLegacyLens` assertions, never by `ReviewRoles` literals. The §6.1 preamble's search finds this file on the `TranslateLegacyLens` token, not on a `ReviewRoles` one, so the item's stated reason and the derivation that produced it disagree. A decomposer reading item 3 scopes the edit into the §2.2 type-change task — and per CLAUDE.md's own "a change and the test it invalidates belong to the SAME task" rule, misattributing which change invalidates a test is exactly what produces a dependency graph that looks correct and cannot be executed.

resolved.evidence: Same defect as finding 4, same fix — the entry now describes what the file actually contains.

suggestion: Rewrite item 3 as: "`internal/engine/lens_shim_test.go` — asserts `TranslateLegacyLens`'s returned override map as `[]string` literals. Invalidated only if §2.2's open choice changes that return type; under the adapt-at-the-call-site branch it is unaffected. Its single `fm.ReviewRoles` use is a `require.NotEmpty` that survives the element-type change." Whichever branch the implementer picks, the task that picks it owns this file.

finding: The new `enabled: null` carve-out lives only in §2.2's first paragraph and is contradicted in isolation by the unqualified rule three lines later ("A non-boolean `enabled` is a lint warning and is ignored"); YAML null is non-boolean, so an implementer writing the type switch from line 40 alone warns on `enabled: null`. No §6 item pins the carve-out, while every sibling parse rule has one (item 3 for `enabled: true`, item 4 for the quoted-string non-boolean, item 5 for the unpermitted key). The round-11 finding this repair answers named §6 explicitly ("Nothing in §6 pins either"), so the prose half was repaired and the test half was not — the same half-fix shape the project recorded as a lesson after round 7. Verified the sibling precedent is real: parseRoleOverrides treats a nil focus as empty with no warning (internal/engine/frontmatter.go:172-177), so §2.2's claim about `focus: null` is accurate; only its guard is missing.

resolved.evidence: Fixed. §2.2's rule now reads "A non-nil, non-boolean `enabled`" with the nil case named inline, so the carve-out three lines above is no longer contradicted in isolation; §6 item 14 gives it a test.

suggestion: Add a §6 item: `enabled: null` and a valueless `enabled:` leave the role active, emit no warning, and are indistinguishable from an absent key. Qualify line 40's rule to "A non-null, non-boolean `enabled`" so the two sentences do not have to be read together to get the right behaviour.

finding: The new clause "the audit caller additionally feeds it §2.5's `spec-coverage` refusal, which the review caller cannot trip (§6 item 10)" is right as a wiring statement, but the item it cites justifies the same conclusion by a different, corpus-contingent mechanism: item 10 says "`tp.review_roles` naming `spec-coverage` takes the 'matches no active role' path instead" and §2.5 line 61 says "as `tp.review_roles` naming it always does". Role ids are project-authored filenames and only `regression` is reserved, so a project may author .tp/reviewers/spec-coverage.json. Against that corpus §2.3's own general rule drops the role (removed from the panel, one `disabled-by-spec` skipped_roles row), while item 10's "instead" and §2.5's "always" say it warns and stays active — an observable divergence on the review phase, and item 10 is a test item, so an implementer taking it literally special-cases the id and leaves active a role the spec asked to deactivate. §2.3's own wiring already establishes the review caller cannot trip the refusal, so the citation does not need the corpus claim.

resolved.evidence: ACCEPTED with justification (low, non-blocking). The clause is right as a wiring statement and cites §6 item 10 for the corpus-contingent half. Restating the contingency at both sites would duplicate a condition that item 10 already pins with its fixture, and this spec has lost two mechanisms to duplicated normative text drifting apart.

suggestion: Leave §2.3's wiring reason standing on its own and qualify the two corpus-contingent sentences: item 10 and §2.5 line 61 should read "takes the 'matches no active role' path whenever the reviewer corpus has no active `spec-coverage` role — as no default corpus does; where a project authors one, `enabled: false` drops it like any other reviewer, since only the auditor drop set reaches the refusal".
